description: Why does hip power matter more than muscle? Because the tape measure, the stopwatch and the wall have never once asked how big your legs look. Take the broad jump test and learn the argument that should reorganize your entire training life: performance is power per kilo, and you are built for it.

scenes.narration: The broad jump, one more time, because this episode needs its evidence fresh. Toes behind the line, full arm swing, quarter dip, explode, stick it, measure to the nearest heel. Three jumps, best distance is your number today. Keep it close, because we are about to have an argument, and your number is exhibit A. The argument is the title of this episode: why your hip power matters more than muscle. Not matters instead of muscle, not muscle is useless, but matters more, for the things legs are actually for: jumping, sprinting, cutting, climbing, playing, lasting. The fitness world grades legs in a mirror. The physical world grades them in meters, seconds and centimeters, and those two report cards routinely name different winners. You have probably stood next to a guy with legs twice your size and wondered what the point of yours is. By the end of this episode you will know the point, in numbers: power is force divided by bodyweight and delivered in a fraction of a second, and on that formula, your build is not the underdog. It is the favorite that has not started training yet.

scenes.label: THE LINE MUSCLE CANNOT BUY
scenes.narration: The line is two meters, two forty for the elite, and here is the fact that frames this whole episode: knowing a man's jump distance tells you more about his athletic future than knowing his leg size, his squat, or his weight. Coaches test jumps precisely because power per kilo predicts sprinting, game speed and agility better than any gym number. Muscle size, meanwhile, predicts mostly muscle size. This is not an insult to muscle; strength is the raw material power is refined from, and we will train it in this episode too. But raw material is not the product. A warehouse of bricks is not a house, and a thigh full of potential force that arrives slowly and drags extra bodyweight with it is not performance. Your number today is a performance grade. The rest of the episode is the argument for reorganizing your training around it.
scenes.sub: under 1.6 m: power untrained - over 2.4 m: elite power per kilo

lines: Power = force x speed, divided by your mass.
Muscle only supplies one of the three terms.
beats.title: THE POWER EQUATION

beats.text: SIZE IS AN INGREDIENT, NOT THE MEAL

scenes.narration: Write the equation down, because your whole training life should be organized by it. Power equals force times speed, and in any bodyweight sport, what matters is that product divided by the mass it must move. Three terms. Muscle size contributes to exactly one of them, force, and even there it is only a partial shareholder, because neural recruitment decides how much of your muscle's force you can actually access in a quarter-second. Speed of contraction is a nervous system quality. Mass is the denominator, the tax every other term pays. Now grade the typical gym career against the equation: years spent growing the force term slowly, while the speed term goes untrained and the mass term grows against you, because muscle is heavy and every kilo of it must be carried by the power it creates. The hip sits at the center of the winning strategy because it is where the largest force in the body meets the fastest delivery. Train the product, not the ingredient. That is the whole argument in one sentence.

The evidence for the argument is the entire practice of professional sport. Scouts and performance labs test vertical and broad jumps obsessively because those numbers forecast who will accelerate, who will win aerial contests, who will change direction at speed. Nobody at that level tests thigh circumference. Research comparing athletes keeps finding the same pattern: relative power, power per kilo of bodyweight, separates performance levels far better than absolute strength or size, because sport is played by moving your own body against gravity and opponents, not by posing it. There is also the aging argument, the one nobody makes to twenty-year-olds: muscle size fades fast when training stops, but power trained through the nervous system, the skill of firing fast, persists remarkably. Build your legs around power and you are building the quality that performs now and retires last.

beats.text: BUILD THE BASE, SPEND IT FAST

scenes.narration: The deep dive is the honest counterweight, because an argument you cannot steelman is just marketing. Muscle matters: force is a real term in the equation, and a guy with no strength base has nothing for his nervous system to spend. This is why the protocol ahead includes heavy hinge work and why this channel will never tell you size is worthless. The claim is about priority and proportion. Most skinny guys train as if force were ninety percent of performance, spending years on the slowest-improving term while the fastest-improving terms, firing speed and the denominator they already own, sit untouched. Rebalance the portfolio: keep building the base, but spend serious weekly effort on expressing it fast, and judge the whole program by performance numbers, jumps, sprints, times, not by the mirror's quarterly report. Muscle is the savings account. Power is the income. Live on the income.

beats.text: EVERY TERM IS TRAINABLE EXCEPT THE TAX

scenes.narration: Your advantage in the power equation is structural, and it is the strongest one in this season. Of the three terms, two are trainable for everyone: force and firing speed, where you can match anyone's work ethic and most of anyone's results. The third term, the mass in the denominator, is the one your rivals cannot train away, because their size is the point of their training. Every kilo they add to look powerful taxes the power they were chasing. You start with the denominator already optimized and get to spend all your effort on the numerator. This is why lean athletes dominate the jumping and sprinting record books across a century of sport, and why your ceiling in the performance world is not set by your frame. Your frame is the qualifying credential. The only question the tape asks is whether you trained the product.

Now we train the product together. Four rounds: twenty seconds of maximal broad jumps, full swing, stick the landing, walk back and reset. Rest forty seconds between rounds. Every rep is the equation being solved at full speed, so no tired reps are allowed in the building.

beats.text: HINGES FOR FORCE, TWICE A WEEK

scenes.narration: Your protocol, the equation turned into a week. Twice a week, force: heavy hinges and squats, sets of five, full rest, the savings account being funded. Twice a week, speed: broad jumps and sprints in small, maximal, fully-recovered doses, the income being earned. Once a week, test something and write it down, a jump, a twenty, a hop count, because the program is graded by performance numbers or it is graded by nothing. And one rule for your head: the mirror is retired as a leg judge. It had decades to make its case and it never once predicted a sprint. Your legs will still grow on this program, by the way, as a side effect of heavy hinges and hard jumps. They will just grow as a consequence of performance instead of as a substitute for it, which is the order nature intended.

So, your distance, exhibit A in the case for power. Under one sixty: your numerator is untrained, both terms of it, and the equation says that is the most improvable position in the sport, because beginners gain force and speed simultaneously. One sixty to two meters: the product is forming; the protocol's balance is exactly your next step. Two meters to two forty: you are living proof of the argument, performance a mirror would never have predicted. Over two forty: elite power per kilo, the full equation solved at a high level. Put your distance in the comments, just the number, and retest in thirty days: same line, same honest heel. Then look at the two report cards side by side, the tape's and the mirror's, and notice which one your training answers to now.

Thirty days from now, same line, same tape, bring me a longer jump and we will check what it did to the rest of your numbers. Subscribe, and keep your number safe until then. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: Why Your hip power Matter More Than Muscle (The broad jump Episode)
